title: The traveler's hymns
hook: a Guru on the road east, and a hymn that asks the mind to take shelter

segments.voice: Yesterday, suffering calmly, and a carpenter's bubble. Your line was level. When something tipped you, did the bubble come back? Day one thousand two hundred eighteen.

Dust on the road. A river to cross by boat, then another. Days of walking and riding, nights in the homes of strangers who become sangat by morning. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Tegh Bahadur as a traveler, journeying east, through the lands toward Bengal and Assam, visiting Sikhs and meeting seekers along the way. Tradition says his son, the future tenth Guru, was born at Patna while he was away on those journeys. A Guru on the road, far from home. And some of his hymns, tradition says, belong to those roads.
screen: `DUST, RIVERS, STRANGERS' HOMES.` → `EAST, TOWARD BENGAL AND ASSAM.` → `HYMNS FROM THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, an honest thing. The Guru Granth Sahib arranges his hymns by raga, by musical mode, not by place. It doesn't print a map beside each one. So when people link a hymn to a journey, that's tradition and memory, not a label in the book. But listen to what his hymns sound like, and the road is there. One, in Raga Sorath, paraphrased, begins: O mind, take the shelter of the Lord's Name; remembering it, bad thinking is destroyed, and the highest state is reached. Shelter. In Gurmukhi, ot. On a road, it's a word that makes sense. On a long road you don't need a palace; you need somewhere to stand out of the rain. And notice who the hymn talks to. Not the crowd. Not a king. O mind. It turns and speaks to the one companion who comes on every journey, the voice in your own head. On the road, that's often the only one listening. So a traveler's hymn is a hymn you can carry. No building required, no instrument, no gathering. Just a line, and a mind to say it to. That's prayer on the road. Now, this has been a week of travel too. We started with Guru Arjan the editor, choosing carefully, and closed his life: poet and builder. Then we turned to the ninth Guru. Neither fear nor frighten. Home, held lightly. Their faith, their right. Level. And today, the road. Different roads, one shelter.
screen: `ARRANGED BY RAGA, NOT BY PLACE.` · `O MIND, TAKE SHELTER.` · `A HYMN YOU CAN CARRY.` · `A WEEK ON THE ROAD.` · then, large: `PRAYER ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray on a journey. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the next trip you'll make, even a short one. The drive to work. The bus. The walk to the store. Ride it in your mind: the first turn, the traffic, the place you usually start scrolling. Now pick one spot on that route to be your shelter, a light, a corner, a bridge. When you reach it, you'll speak to your own mind for one breath. If you pray, the word can be Waheguru. If you don't, simply: here, now. The bell holds the time.
The traveler's hymns. Guru Tegh Bahadur journeyed east, and his hymns speak to the mind, offering a shelter you can carry anywhere. Today's word.
Your line: prayer on the road. Today, when you reach the spot you chose, take the shelter: one breath, one word, then keep going. Day one thousand two hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras stand at places tradition links to Guru Tegh Bahadur's journeys, including Patna Sahib, and Sikhs sing his hymns in kirtan; some Sikhs also recite or listen to gurbani while traveling.

original.note: shelter, refuge; the Sorath hymn asks the mind to take the shelter of the Lord's Name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the traveler's hymns are about places he visited.
what it means: hymns you can carry, spoken to your own mind, a shelter on any road.
what a scholar hears: the Granth orders hymns by raga, so linking a hymn to a journey rests on tradition, not on the book.
